```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo       = TRUE,
  message    = FALSE,
  warning    = FALSE,
  cache      = TRUE,
  cache.lazy = FALSE,   # model objects are large; lazy loading fails on them
  autodep    = TRUE,    # let knitr work out chunk dependencies from object usage
  comment    = "#>",
  fig.align  = "center",
  dpi        = 110
)
options(width = 110, scipen = 6)   # keep counts readable, but let tiny p-values
                                   # stay in scientific notation rather than print as 0

library(tidyverse)
library(survival)
library(broom)
library(coxme)
library(kableExtra)
library(here)      # portable paths anchored at the repo root (.Rproj / .git)

BASE <- here("data", "processed")   # repo-root/data/processed, wherever the repo lives

# One consistent table style for the whole document.
show_tbl <- function(x, caption = NULL, digits = 3) {
  kbl(x, caption = caption, digits = digits) %>%
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                  full_width = FALSE, position = "left", font_size = 13)
}

# HR = exp(coef); returns NA if the term isn't in that model.
hr <- function(fit, term) {
  b <- coef(fit)[term]
  if (is.na(b)) NA_real_ else round(exp(b), 3)
}

# p-values here span 0.97 down to ~1e-11. Rounding to 3 dp would print the tiny
# ones as "0.000", which reads as "exactly zero" - so anything under 0.001 is
# shown in scientific notation instead.
fmt_p <- function(p) {
  ifelse(is.na(p), NA_character_,
         ifelse(p < 0.001, formatC(p, format = "e", digits = 2),
                           formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3)))
}
```

# What this document is {.unnumbered}

This is the modelling half of my thesis, run end to end in one place.
Scripts 1-5 build the data; everything from here on fits, diagnoses and
validates the models. I moved it out of the numbered R files and into R
Markdown so that the reasoning, the code and the output sit next to each
other, when I write the thesis I want to be reading my own justification
alongside the number it produced, not flipping between a script and a
console log.

Does an NBA player's recent workload and schedule congestion carry
signal that assist in indicating when a player is at elevated risk of
being injured, and how much of any such signal is real physiology versus
an artefact of who is fit enough to be playing in the first place?

::: {.alert .alert-info}
Every model here is re-fitted from `cox_ready_2021-26.rds` when this
document knits, nothing is read back from a saved model object. Chunks
are cached, so the first knit is slow (the frailty model and the
cross-validation folds dominate).
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# The modelling dataset

```{r load-data}
cox <- readRDS(file.path(BASE, "cox_ready_2021-26.rds"))

data_summary <- tibble(
  Quantity = c("Player-game intervals (rows)", "Distinct players", "Seasons",
               "New-injury events (primary outcome)",
               "  - soft-tissue", "  - load-linked structural", "  - random-impact",
               "All-injury events (new + reaggravation)",
               "  - soft-tissue", "  - load-linked structural", "  - random-impact"),
  Value = c(
    format(nrow(cox), big.mark = ","),
    format(n_distinct(cox$PLAYER_ID), big.mark = ","),
    sprintf("%d (%s to %s)", n_distinct(cox$SEASON), min(cox$SEASON), max(cox$SEASON)),
    format(sum(cox$event), big.mark = ","),
    format(sum(cox$event_soft), big.mark = ","),
    format(sum(cox$event_load), big.mark = ","),
    format(sum(cox$event_impact), big.mark = ","),
    format(sum(cox$event_recurrent), big.mark = ","),
    format(sum(cox$event_soft_recurrent), big.mark = ","),
    format(sum(cox$event_load_recurrent), big.mark = ","),
    format(sum(cox$event_impact_recurrent), big.mark = ",")
  )
)
show_tbl(data_summary, "The counting-process dataset")
```

Each row is one player-game interval `(t_start, t_stop]` with an event
indicator. The clock is **game number within a season**, and a player
only contributes rows while they are genuinely *at risk*, once an injury
starts, the remaining missed games are removed and they re-enter when
they play again. Otherwise I would be counting a player as "surviving"
games they were never available for.

I have 3,257 new-injury events across 1,029 players. Large enough that
**p-values stop being informative on their own**, which is a theme I
return to repeatedly below. At this sample size a trivially small effect
will still return p \< 0.001, so throughout I read effect size first and
significance second.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Stage 0 - Covariate screening

Cox models are unstable when two covariates carry nearly the same
information, coefficients effects get split between them, standard
errors inflate, and signs can flip. I have several rolling windows of
the same underlying quantity (7-day, 28-day and 42-day minutes, for
instance). I screen for it *before* fitting, rather than fitting first
and rationalising afterwards.

I use **Spearman** rather than Pearson because these workload
distributions are skewed and I care about monotone redundancy, not
linear redundancy.

```{r stage0-screening}
candidates <- c(
  "ACWR_MIN", "ROLLING_MIN_7D", "ROLLING_MIN_28D", "ROLLING_MIN_42D",
  "SEASON_CUMULATIVE_MIN", "ROLLING_GAMES_7D", "ROLLING_GAMES_28D",
  "ROLLING_LOAD_7D", "ROLLING_LOAD_28D", "ACWR_LOAD",
  "ROLLING_INTENSITY_7D", "ROLLING_INTENSITY_28D", "INTENSITY",
  "ROLLING_DIST_7D", "ROLLING_DIST_28D", "SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST",
  "TEAM_DAYS_REST", "ROLLING_B2B_7D", "ROLLING_B2B_28D",
  "PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP_GAME_NUMBER", "MIN", "DISTANCE",
  "SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE", "CAREER_GAMES_MISSED", "SEASON_GAMES_MISSED",
  "PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON", "PLAYER_AGE_AT_GAME", "HEIGHT_INCHES", "WEIGHT",
  "PCT_THROUGH_SEASON"
)
candidates <- candidates[candidates %in% names(cox)]

cor_mat <- cor(cox[candidates], use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "spearman")
high    <- which(abs(cor_mat) > 0.8 & upper.tri(cor_mat), arr.ind = TRUE)

collinear <- tibble(
  Variable_1 = rownames(cor_mat)[high[, 1]],
  Variable_2 = colnames(cor_mat)[high[, 2]],
  Spearman_r = round(cor_mat[high], 3)
) %>% arrange(desc(abs(Spearman_r)))

show_tbl(collinear, "Collinear pairs (|Spearman r| > 0.8) - only one of each enters the model")
```

## What it shows

23 pairs breach the 0.8 threshold, and they cluster into a few obvious
families: the overlapping minutes windows, the career-length variables,
and the in-game effort measures. For each I keep **one** on
interpretability grounds rather than statistical ones:

-   `SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE` over age and draft year: experience is the
    construct in the literature (the Russell inverted-U).
-   `ROLLING_MIN_28D` over the 42-day window: 28 days is the
    conventional chronic window in the ACWR literature, so it keeps my
    results comparable to prior work.
-   `MIN` for in-game effort.

Two specific exclusions worth recording, because both were judgement
calls:

-   **`ROLLING_GAMES_28D` is dropped** (r = 0.86 with chronic minutes).
    It was redundant *and* null when fitted, so nothing is lost.
-   **`ROLLING_GAMES_7D` is kept.** Its correlation with 7-day minutes
    sits under 0.8, and it separates *frequency* from *volume*, playing
    four games in a week is a different stimulus from playing the same
    minutes across two.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Stage 1 - Nested models

My hypothesis is ordered, so the model build is ordered too. I add
covariates in three **domain blocks**, workload, then schedule
congestion, then player context, and ask at each, whether the new domain
earns its place. That structure answers "which domain matters", rather
than producing one flat model where I'd be picking through 24
individually significant coefficients.

Three specification choices carry the design, and each is a deliberate
answer to a feature of this data:

| Choice | Why it is there |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `Surv(t_start, t_stop, event)` | Counting-process form, so covariates can change every game. injured this season y/n model would collapse the season to one outcome and be blind to *when* risk moves. |
| `strata(SEASON)` | Each season gets its own baseline hazard. The COVID-adjacent seasons had a genuinely different shape, and I don't want that contaminating the covariate effects. I assume workload *acts* the same way each season, not that each season is equally dangerous. |
| `cluster(PLAYER_ID)` | LeBron contributes \~332 rows that are one repeatedly-observed person, not 332 independent facts. Without this the standard errors are far too narrow. |

I also **z-score every continuous covariate**, so each hazard ratio
reads as "per 1 standard deviation increase". That is what makes it
legitimate to say chronic load matters more than travel, otherwise I'd
be comparing an effect measured in minutes against one measured in
kilometres.

```{r zscore}
z <- function(x) as.numeric(scale(x))

cox <- cox %>%
  mutate(
    # Workload - minutes & intensity -based
    z_ROLLING_MIN_7D   = z(ROLLING_MIN_7D),
    z_ROLLING_MIN_28D  = z(ROLLING_MIN_28D),
    z_ACWR_MIN         = z(ACWR_MIN),
    z_ROLLING_GAMES_7D = z(ROLLING_GAMES_7D),
    z_MIN              = z(MIN),
    z_PREV_GAME_MIN    = z(PREV_GAME_MIN),   
    z_PREV_2GAME_MIN   = z(PREV_2GAME_MIN), 
    z_ROLLING_INTENSITY_7D   = z(ROLLING_INTENSITY_7D),
    z_ROLLING_INTENSITY_28D  = z(ROLLING_INTENSITY_28D),
    z_INTENSITY              = z(INTENSITY),
    # Workload - on-court tracking load (used in Stage 5)
    z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D  = z(ROLLING_LOAD_7D),
    z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D = z(ROLLING_LOAD_28D),
    z_ACWR_LOAD        = z(ACWR_LOAD),
    z_PREV_GAME_DISTANCE   = z(PREV_GAME_DISTANCE),
    z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE  = z(PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE),
    # Travel
    z_ROLLING_DIST_7D        = z(ROLLING_DIST_7D),
    z_ROLLING_DIST_28D       = z(ROLLING_DIST_28D),
    z_SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST = z(SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST),
    # Schedule congestion
    z_IS_B2B = z(IS_B2B),
    z_ROLLING_B2B_7D               = z(ROLLING_B2B_7D),
    z_ROLLING_B2B_28D              = z(ROLLING_B2B_28D),
    z_PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP_GAME_NUMBER = z(PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP_GAME_NUMBER),
    z_TEAM_DAYS_REST               = z(TEAM_DAYS_REST),
    # Player context
    z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE     = z(SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE),
    z_CAREER_GAMES_MISSED   = z(CAREER_GAMES_MISSED),
    z_PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON = z(PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON),
    z_PCT_THROUGH_SEASON    = z(PCT_THROUGH_SEASON),
    z_HEIGHT_INCHES         = z(HEIGHT_INCHES),
    z_WEIGHT                = z(WEIGHT)
  )
```

```{r model-specs, dependson="zscore"}
surv_lhs <- "Surv(t_start, t_stop, event)"
rhs_tail <- "strata(SEASON) + cluster(PLAYER_ID)"

fit_cox <- function(covariate_terms, lhs = surv_lhs) {
  f <- as.formula(paste0(lhs, " ~ ", paste(covariate_terms, collapse = " + "),
                         " + ", rhs_tail))
  coxph(f, data = cox, ties = "efron")
}

# Workload block - ON-COURT LOAD (tracking distance). I use load rather than minutes
# as my exposure: distance covered is what the body actually absorbed, the sports-
# science "external load", whereas minutes is a coaching decision. Load and minutes
# are ~0.995 collinear here, so this doesn't change discrimination - I verify that
# with a minutes robustness fit below - it just puts the better construct in front.
m1_terms <- c(
  "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D",         # acute on-court load (distance)
  "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D",        # chronic on-court load (distance)
  "z_ACWR_LOAD",               # acute:chronic load ratio
  "z_ROLLING_GAMES_7D",        # acute games played (frequency)
  "z_ROLLING_DIST_7D",         # acute travel load
  "z_ROLLING_DIST_28D",        # chronic travel load
  "z_SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST",  # season-long accumulated travel
  "z_PREV_GAME_DISTANCE",      # in-game load, last played game (lag-1, load-management signal)
  "z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE"      # in-game load, 2 games back (lag-2, prospective fatigue spike)
)

schedule_added <- c(
  "z_IS_B2B","z_ROLLING_B2B_7D", "z_ROLLING_B2B_28D",
  "z_PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP_GAME_NUMBER", "z_TEAM_DAYS_REST", "IS_PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP"
)

context_added <- c(
  "z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE", "I(z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE^2)",   # Russell inverted-U
  "z_CAREER_GAMES_MISSED",                             # career durability
  "z_PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON", "RECENT_RETURN",          # prior-injury history
  "z_PCT_THROUGH_SEASON", "IS_POST_ALLSTAR",           # season timing
  "PLAYED_PRESEASON", "z_HEIGHT_INCHES", "z_WEIGHT"
)

m2_terms <- c(m1_terms, schedule_added)
m3_terms <- c(m2_terms, context_added)

# The minutes-based counterpart of the full Model 3, kept only for the robustness
# check: same specification with minutes swapped in for load - including the same lag-1
# + lag-2 treatment of the in-game term, so the comparison is apples-to-apples.
m3_terms_min <- c("z_ROLLING_MIN_7D", "z_ROLLING_MIN_28D", "z_ACWR_MIN",
                  "z_ROLLING_GAMES_7D", "z_ROLLING_DIST_7D", "z_ROLLING_DIST_28D",
                  "z_SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST", "z_PREV_GAME_MIN", "z_PREV_2GAME_MIN",
                  schedule_added, context_added)
```

**A note on the in-game load term.** Rather than the current game's
distance, I use two lagged versions: the last game played
(`PREV_GAME_DISTANCE`, lag-1) and two games back (`PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE`,
lag-2). The current game's distance is contemporaneous with the injury
and reverse-caused (a player who breaks down logs a low distance in the
game it happens) so it reads protective for the wrong reason. Both lags
are known before the interval opens, so they are genuinely prospective,
and they separate two signals: the last game carries the load-management
pattern (the game before a breakdown is often a managed, compromised
one, so lag-1 reads protective), while two games back sits before that
compromise and reads as the harmful fatigue spike a real overuse
mechanism should produce.

*I validated that lag-2 survives out-of-sample and is not just
re-expressing the rolling load (VIF ≈ 3) before adopting it. The
trade-off is coverage, a player's first two games each season have no
lag-2 and drop from these models.*

A note on the schedule block, I included **both** the accumulated
congestion dose (rolling back-to-back counts, road-trip game number)
**and** the point-in-time flags (`IS_B2B`, `IS_PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP`). The
accumulated versions are the exposure measure. The point-in-time flags
are contaminated by coaching decisions, because a coach rests an at-risk
player tonight. I keep them in so the contrast is visible in the results
table rather than hidden by dropping them, and I mark them as
selection-biased everywhere they appear.

## Model 1 - Workload

```{r m1, dependson="model-specs"}
m1 <- fit_cox(m1_terms)
summary(m1)
```

## Model 2 - Workload + Schedule

```{r m2, dependson="model-specs"}
m2 <- fit_cox(m2_terms)
summary(m2)
```

## Model 3 - Workload + Schedule + Player context

```{r m3, dependson="model-specs"}
m3 <- fit_cox(m3_terms)
summary(m3)
```

## Does each domain earn its place?

The classical likelihood-ratio test does not work here. LRT compares two
log-likelihoods, but `cluster(PLAYER_ID)` doesn't change the likelihood,
it only replaces the variance estimate afterwards. So an LRT would use
the naive likelihood and ignores the correlation corrected for. Instead
I use a **robust Wald test** on the block of newly-added coefficients,
built from the clustered variance-covariance matrix, plus the change in
concordance.

```{r nested-tests, dependson=c("m1","m2","m3")}
# Joint H0 test that the coefficients in a model are all zero, using the
# robust (clustered) covariance. Small p => the block contributes beyond the prior model.
robust_wald <- function(model, added_terms) {
  cf   <- coef(model)
  norm <- function(s) gsub("\\s", "", s)      # I(x^2) spacing varies; match robustly
  idx  <- which(norm(names(cf)) %in% norm(added_terms))
  V    <- vcov(model)[idx, idx, drop = FALSE] # robust vcov of just those coefficients
  b    <- cf[idx]
  stat <- as.numeric(t(b) %*% solve(V) %*% b) # Wald statistic: b' V^-1 b
  tibble(block_df = length(idx), wald_chisq = round(stat, 2),
         p_value  = signif(pchisq(stat, length(idx), lower.tail = FALSE), 4))
}

nested <- bind_rows(
  robust_wald(m2, schedule_added) %>% mutate(block = "Schedule (added to Model 1)"),
  robust_wald(m3, context_added)  %>% mutate(block = "Player context (added to Model 2)")
) %>%
  select(block, block_df, wald_chisq, p_value) %>%
  mutate(p_value = fmt_p(p_value))

concordance_progression <- tibble(
  Model = c("Model 1 - workload", "Model 2 - + schedule", "Model 3 - + player context"),
  Concordance = c(summary(m1)$concordance[1],
                  summary(m2)$concordance[1],
                  summary(m3)$concordance[1]) %>% round(4)
)

show_tbl(nested, "Robust Wald tests on each added block")
show_tbl(concordance_progression, "Discrimination as each domain is added")
```

```{r m3-hr, dependson="m3"}
m3_tidy <- tidy(m3, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(effect_size = abs(estimate - 1)) %>%
  arrange(desc(effect_size)) %>%
  select(term, HR = estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value, robust.se) %>%
  mutate(p.value = fmt_p(p.value))

show_tbl(m3_tidy, "Model 3 - hazard ratios, sorted by effect size (not by p)")
```

## Does the exposure choice matter?

I report on-court load, but load and minutes are \~0.995 collinear here,
so a fair question is whether anything hinges on that choice. It does
not. Refitting the *whole* of Model 3 with minutes swapped in for load
leaves discrimination and the headline hazard ratios essentially
unchanged.

```{r robustness-minutes, dependson="model-specs"}
m3_min <- fit_cox(m3_terms_min)   # same Model 3, minutes in place of load

robust_tab <- tibble(
  Metric = c("Concordance", "Chronic workload HR (per SD)",
             "Acute workload HR (per SD)", "ACWR HR (per SD)"),
  `Load (reported)` = c(
    round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 4),
    hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"), hr(m3, "z_ACWR_LOAD")),
  `Minutes (robustness)` = c(
    round(summary(m3_min)$concordance[1], 4),
    hr(m3_min, "z_ROLLING_MIN_28D"), hr(m3_min, "z_ROLLING_MIN_7D"), hr(m3_min, "z_ACWR_MIN"))
)
show_tbl(robust_tab, "Robustness - on-court load vs minutes give the same answer")
```

So the exposure choice is not driving the result. I lead with load
because it is the better *construct*, what the body absorbed rather than
what the coach decided.

## What it shows

Both blocks earn their place, and concordance climbs at each step to
`r round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 3)`. That means given two
comparable player-intervals, the model ranks the one that actually gets
injured as higher-risk about
`r round(100 * summary(m3)$concordance[1])`% of the time, against 50% by
chance. For a model built entirely from **public box-score and schedule
data**, with no access to GPS, medical screening or training-load data,
I think that is the honest near ceiling rather than a disappointment,
and establishing that ceiling is itself a useful finding for anyone
deciding whether public data is sufficient for this task.

Chronic 28-day load is the headline effect at **HR
`r round(summary(m3)$conf.int["z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D", 1], 1)` per SD**. I
want to also flag as not a finding is that several point-in-time
covariates come out looking strongly protective. Rest days and the
back-to-back flag both do this. Playing a back-to-back is *safer*, which
is doesnt make sense at first. It is **health-gating**: coaches rest
players who are carrying something, so "played on low rest" selects for
players who were fit that night. This is why the accumulated measures
are the ones I interpret.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Stage 2 - The proportional-hazards assumption

The Cox model assumes each covariate's effect is **constant over time**,
that heavy chronic load is as dangerous in game 70 as in game 10. That
is a strong assumption and it is testable. I use scaled Schoenfeld
residuals (`cox.zph`), which essentially ask whether the covariate
values of the players who actually fail drift systematically as the
season progresses.

This stage is a core of the thesis, a violation here is a finding. It
would mean a risk factor intensifies or fades across a season, a dynamic
that only the time-to-event framing can surface at all. So I went in
genuinely hoping to find one.

I set `transform = "identity"` so the time axis stays raw **game
number**. The default Kaplan-Meier transform would compress the axis in
a way that makes the plotted trend hard to reconcile with any
time-interaction I might fit afterwards.

```{r ph-tests, dependson=c("m1","m2","m3")}
zph1 <- cox.zph(m1, transform = "identity")
zph2 <- cox.zph(m2, transform = "identity")
zph3 <- cox.zph(m3, transform = "identity")

zph3_tab <- as.data.frame(zph3$table) %>%
  rownames_to_column("term") %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(flag = if_else(term != "GLOBAL" & p < 0.05, "** VIOLATES", "")) %>%
  arrange(term == "GLOBAL", p)

plot_terms <- zph3_tab %>% filter(term != "GLOBAL") %>% pull(term)  # GLOBAL has no curve to plot

zph3_tab %>%
  mutate(chisq = round(chisq, 2), p = fmt_p(p)) %>%
  show_tbl("Model 3 - proportional-hazards test (scaled Schoenfeld residuals)")
```

`r sum(zph3_tab$flag != "")` individual covariates flagged at p \< 0.05
(the two lag in-game load terms among them, at p ≈ 0.002 and 0.007).

## The plots, which is where the decision actually got made

The p-value only tells me a slope isn't exactly zero, at
`r format(m3$nevent, big.mark = ",")` events, a near-flat line will
still test significant. The *shape* is what matters, so I plot every
term. A flat line means the assumption holds; a sloping line means the
effect drifts.

```{r schoenfeld-plots, dependson="ph-tests", fig.height=4.2, fig.width=7.5, results="hold"}
for (v in plot_terms) {
  idx <- which(rownames(zph3$table) == v)
  plot(zph3[idx], resid = FALSE, lwd = 2, col = "steelblue",
       main = paste0("Schoenfeld: ", v, "  (effect vs game number)"))
  abline(h = 0, col = "grey50", lty = 2)
}
```

## What it shows, and why I remedied nothing

Covariates drift gently by a comparable amount. That points to one
systematic cause acting on all of them, not to a handful of independent
time-varying risk factors, and fitting a separate time-interaction to
each of a common cause would be modelling the symptom.

because chronic load is PH-stable, a bad chronic load is a bad chronic
load regardless of when in the season it occurs. That is a cleaner and
more actionable message than a time-varying effect would have been.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Stage 3 - Reporting and calibration

Using Model 3, this stage produces the numbers that go in the results:
how well the model discriminates, whether its risk score correctly
orders risk, and the final hazard-ratio table organised by domain.

I dont produce a classic absolute-risk calibration curve, and that is a
design consequence, with `strata(SEASON)` there are five baseline
hazards rather than one, and each row is a game-interval rather than a
person, so "predicted 30-day risk" is not well defined here. What my
design supports, is relative-hazard calibration: group intervals by risk
score and check that the observed event rate climbs across the groups.

```{r calibration, dependson="m3"}
cstat <- summary(m3)$concordance
c_est <- cstat[1]; c_se <- cstat[2]
c_lo  <- c_est - 1.96 * c_se; c_hi <- c_est + 1.96 * c_se

cox_lp <- cox %>%
  mutate(risk_score = as.numeric(predict(m3, newdata = ., type = "lp"))) %>%
  filter(!is.na(risk_score))

calib <- cox_lp %>%
  mutate(risk_group = ntile(risk_score, 10)) %>%
  group_by(risk_group) %>%
  summarise(
    n_intervals     = n(),
    events          = sum(event),
    event_rate_1k   = round(1000 * sum(event) / n(), 2),
    mean_risk_score = round(mean(risk_score), 3),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

mono <- cor(calib$risk_group, calib$event_rate_1k, method = "spearman")
show_tbl(calib, "Relative-hazard calibration: observed event rate by risk-score decile")
```

```{r calibration-plot, dependson="calibration", fig.height=4.5, fig.width=7}
ggplot(calib, aes(risk_group, event_rate_1k)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue", size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  labs(title = "Observed injury rate rises monotonically with predicted risk",
       subtitle = paste0("Spearman correlation with decile rank = ", round(mono, 3)),
       x = "Risk-score decile (1 = lowest predicted risk)",
       y = "Observed events per 1,000 intervals") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

```{r hr-table, dependson="m3"}
domain_map <- tribble(
  ~term,                            ~domain,          ~label,
  "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D",              "Workload",       "Acute on-court load (7d)",
  "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D",             "Workload",       "Chronic on-court load (28d)",
  "z_ACWR_LOAD",                    "Workload",       "Acute:chronic load ratio",
  "z_ROLLING_GAMES_7D",             "Workload",       "Acute games played (7d)",
  "z_ROLLING_DIST_7D",              "Workload",       "Acute travel load (7d)",
  "z_ROLLING_DIST_28D",             "Workload",       "Chronic travel load (28d)",
  "z_SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST",       "Workload",       "Season cumulative travel",
  "z_PREV_GAME_DISTANCE",           "Workload",       "In-game load, last game *",
  "z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE",          "Workload",       "In-game load, 2 games back",
  "z_ROLLING_B2B_7D",               "Schedule",       "Acute back-to-back dose (7d)",
  "z_ROLLING_B2B_28D",              "Schedule",       "Chronic back-to-back dose (28d)",
  "z_PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP_GAME_NUMBER", "Schedule",       "Road-trip game number",
  "z_TEAM_DAYS_REST",               "Schedule",       "Team days rest *",
  "IS_B2B",                         "Schedule",       "Back-to-back (point-in-time) *",
  "IS_PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP",            "Schedule",       "On road trip (point-in-time) *",
  "z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE",            "Player context", "Experience (seasons)",
  "I(z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE^2)",       "Player context", "Experience squared (inverted-U)",
  "z_CAREER_GAMES_MISSED",          "Player context", "Career games missed (durability)",
  "z_PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON",        "Player context", "Prior injury episodes this season",
  "RECENT_RETURN",                  "Player context", "Recently returned (<=14d)",
  "z_PCT_THROUGH_SEASON",           "Player context", "Season progress",
  "IS_POST_ALLSTAR",                "Player context", "Post-All-Star phase",
  "PLAYED_PRESEASON",               "Player context", "Played pre-season",
  "z_HEIGHT_INCHES",                "Player context", "Height",
  "z_WEIGHT",                       "Player context", "Weight"
)

hr_tab <- tidy(m3, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
  select(term, HR = estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) %>%
  left_join(domain_map, by = "term") %>%
  mutate(domain  = factor(domain, levels = c("Workload", "Schedule", "Player context")),
         across(c(HR, conf.low, conf.high), ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  arrange(domain, desc(abs(log(HR)))) %>%
  mutate(p.value = fmt_p(p.value)) %>%
  select(domain, label, HR, conf.low, conf.high, p.value)

show_tbl(hr_tab, "Final hazard ratios (Model 3), by domain - * = selection-biased")

write.csv(hr_tab, file.path(BASE, "final_hazard_ratios_model3.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

## What it shows

Concordance is `r round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 4)` (95% CI
`r round(summary(m3)$concordance[1] - 1.96 * summary(m3)$concordance[2], 3)`-`r round(summary(m3)$concordance[1] + 1.96 * summary(m3)$concordance[2], 3)`),
and the risk score orders observed hazard almost perfectly across
deciles (Spearman 1). The model reliably sorts high-risk from low-risk
intervals even though it cannot state an absolute probability. For an
operational use case, who should be managed this week, ranking is the
operative quantity anyway.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Stage 4 - Recurrent-events robustness

Model 3 counts only the first new injury of a kind, which throws away
information, players get injured repeatedly, and that repetition is an
aspect the applied literature cares most. Rather than pick one
recurrent-events model and hope, I fit three that make different
assumptions.

-   **Andersen-Gill (AG)** - every event counts, common baseline,
    marginal interpretation. "what raises the hazard of *any* injury
    onset".
-   **PWP gap-time** - stratifies the baseline by event order (1st / 2nd
    / 3rd+) and resets the clock after each event, so risk is "games
    since last injury". "whether a second injury is intrinsically
    different from a first."
-   **Shared frailty** - a per-player random intercept. Its variance θ
    is a direct, single-number measure of unobserved injury-proneness,
    which is the Martin (2021) claim stated as a testable quantity.

```{r ag-model, dependson="model-specs"}
m3_ag <- fit_cox(m3_terms, lhs = "Surv(t_start, t_stop, event_recurrent)")

ag_compare <- full_join(
  tidy(m3,    exponentiate = TRUE) %>% select(term, HR_new_injury = estimate),
  tidy(m3_ag, exponentiate = TRUE) %>% select(term, HR_all_injury = estimate),
  by = "term"
) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))

show_tbl(ag_compare, "Primary (new injury) vs Andersen-Gill (all injury)")
```

```{r pwp, dependson=c("zscore","model-specs")}
# PWP gap-time: within each player-season, ep_order counts which spell this is, and
# the clock restarts at each event so "time" becomes games since the last injury.
pwp <- cox %>%
  arrange(SEASON, PLAYER_ID, t_stop) %>%
  group_by(SEASON, PLAYER_ID) %>%
  mutate(ep_order = 1L + cumsum(lag(event_recurrent, default = 0L))) %>%
  group_by(SEASON, PLAYER_ID, ep_order) %>%
  mutate(gap_stop  = row_number(),
         gap_start = gap_stop - 1L) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(ep_order_capped = factor(pmin(ep_order, 3L), levels = 1:3,
                                  labels = c("1st", "2nd", "3rd+")))

stopifnot(all(pwp$gap_stop > pwp$gap_start), all(pwp$gap_start >= 0))

# Drop prior-episode covariates: the event-order strata and the reset clock already show "how many prior injuries" and "how long since"
pwp_terms <- setdiff(m3_terms, c("z_PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON", "RECENT_RETURN"))

pwp_fit <- coxph(
  as.formula(paste0("Surv(gap_start, gap_stop, event_recurrent) ~ ",
                    paste(pwp_terms, collapse = " + "),
                    " + strata(SEASON, ep_order_capped) + cluster(PLAYER_ID)")),
  data = pwp, ties = "efron"
)

pwp %>%
  group_by(ep_order_capped) %>%
  summarise(rows = n(), events = sum(event_recurrent), .groups = "drop") %>%
  show_tbl("Events by injury-spell stratum")
```

```{r frailty, dependson=c("zscore","model-specs")}
#a random intercept per player.
frail_fit <- coxme(
  as.formula(paste0("Surv(t_start, t_stop, event_recurrent) ~ ",
                    paste(m3_terms, collapse = " + "),
                    " + strata(SEASON) + (1 | PLAYER_ID)")),
  data = cox, ties = "efron"
)

theta    <- as.numeric(unlist(frail_fit$vcoef))[1]
sd_frail <- sqrt(theta)
frail_fit
```

```{r recurrent-compare, dependson=c("ag-model","pwp","frailty")}
headline <- c("z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D", "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D", "z_ACWR_LOAD",
              "z_ROLLING_GAMES_7D", "z_CAREER_GAMES_MISSED", "z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE",
              "z_TEAM_DAYS_REST", "IS_B2B", "z_PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON", "RECENT_RETURN")

hr_from <- function(cf, nm) if (nm %in% names(cf)) round(exp(cf[[nm]]), 3) else NA_real_

compare <- tibble(
  term       = headline,
  HR_AG      = map_dbl(headline, ~ hr_from(coef(m3_ag),    .x)),
  HR_PWP     = map_dbl(headline, ~ hr_from(coef(pwp_fit),  .x)),
  HR_frailty = map_dbl(headline, ~ hr_from(fixef(frail_fit), .x))
)

show_tbl(compare, "Cross-model comparison - AG (marginal) vs PWP (spell strata) vs frailty (conditional)")
```

## What it shows

The headline workload effects hold their shape across all three, the
chronic-load result is not an artefact of how I chose to handle
recurrence.

The frailty variance θ **=** `r round(theta, 3)` is the most interesting
number in this section. On the log-hazard scale that means a player one
SD above average carries roughly `r round(exp(sd_frail), 2)`x the hazard
of an average player, and the 90th versus 10th percentile of proneness
differ by about `r round(exp(2 * qnorm(0.9) * sd_frail), 2)` x (after
adjusting for every covariate in the model). So there is substantial
durable injury-proneness that my public-data covariates do not capture.
That is simultaneously a limitation of my feature set and a direct
quantification of the Martin (2021) claim.

The instructive divergence is `CAREER_GAMES_MISSED`, which moves from
1.11 under AG to 0.967 under frailty (essentially to null). That is not
a contradiction, it is the two models answering different questions. AG
is marginal (across the population, players with more career games
missed are higher risk). Frailty is conditional (holding a player's own
proneness fixed, their career games missed adds nothing). Both are true:
career games missed is largely a *proxy* for the frailty term, so once
frailty is estimated explicitly, the proxy has no work left to do.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Stage 5 - Mechanism, exposure and hazard trajectory

This is the stage that tests my hypothesis hardest, and where I most
expected to be wrong.

The negative control. If workload genuinely *causes* injury, its effect
should depend on injury type: strong for overuse injuries, weaker for
injuries that are essentially random contact events. If instead workload
predicts every injury type equally, including a finger fracture from a
loose ball, then what I am measuring is not fatigue but exposure:
high-load players are on court more, so more things happen to them.

I split into three tiers rather than the obvious two, because my first
attempt was contaminated and I had to redo it. I originally put all
"traumatic" injuries in the control bucket, but ankle sprains were 42%
of that bucket and are plainly load-related, and I had lumped stress
fractures in with acute ones.

1.  **Soft tissue** - hamstring, calf/Achilles, quad, groin. Load
    *should* drive this.
2.  **Load-linked structural** - ACL/PCL, meniscus, ankle sprain, bone
    stress. Load plausibly contributes; a lower-limb stress fracture is
    almost by definition a load injury.
3.  **Random impact** - finger, eye/face, concussion, dislocation. This
    is the **clean control**. Load should have little effect here beyond
    exposure.

I run the split on the same on-court load exposure as the main model, so
all three tiers are compared on identical footing. (I originally also
ran a separate minutes-vs-distance "which exposure predicts better" test
here; that turned out to be the tracking-data artefact discussed below,
so the exposure question is settled and this stage is purely the
mechanism contrast.)

The trajectory. `basehaz()` reads the baseline hazard directly, telling
me when in a season risk elevates for an average player, independent of
any covariate.

```{r mechanism, dependson=c("zscore","model-specs")}
workload_load <- c("z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D", "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D", "z_ACWR_LOAD",
                      "z_ROLLING_GAMES_7D", "z_PREV_GAME_DISTANCE", "z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE",
                      "z_ROLLING_INTENSITY_7D","z_ROLLING_INTENSITY_28D","z_INTENSITY")
shared <- c("z_ROLLING_DIST_7D", "z_ROLLING_DIST_28D", "z_SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST",
            schedule_added, context_added)

fit_outcome <- function(outcome, terms) {
  coxph(as.formula(paste0("Surv(t_start, t_stop, ", outcome, ") ~ ",
                          paste(terms, collapse = " + "), " + ", rhs_tail)),
        data = cox, ties = "efron")
}

m_soft   <- fit_outcome("event_soft",   c(workload_load, shared))  # overuse
m_load  <- fit_outcome("event_load",   c(workload_load, shared))  # load-linked structural
m_impact <- fit_outcome("event_impact", c(workload_load, shared))  # random contact = control
m_soft_load <- fit_outcome("event_soft_load_recurrent", c(workload_load, shared))  # random contact = control

m_soft_recurrent   <- fit_outcome("event_soft_recurrent",   c(workload_load, shared))  # overuse
m_load_recurrent   <- fit_outcome("event_load_recurrent",   c(workload_load, shared))  # load-linked structural
m_soft_load_recurrent <- fit_outcome("event_soft_load_recurrent", c(workload_load, shared))  # random contact = control
m_impact_recurrent <- fit_outcome("event_impact_recurrent", c(workload_load, shared))  # random contact = control

mech_tab <- tibble(
  ` `                = c("Chronic load (28d)", "Acute load (7d)", "Load spike (ACWR)"),
  term               = c("z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D", "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D", "z_ACWR_LOAD"),
  `Soft-tissue`      = map_dbl(term, ~ hr(m_soft,   .x)),
  `Load-linked`      = map_dbl(term, ~ hr(m_load,   .x)),
  `Random-impact`    = map_dbl(term, ~ hr(m_impact, .x))
) %>% select(-term)

# Bottom row: each model's overall discrimination (Harrell's C), so the HRs and the
# ranking ability sit in one place.
mech_tab <- bind_rows(mech_tab, tibble(
  ` `             = "Concordance (C)",
  `Soft-tissue`   = round(summary(m_soft)$concordance[1],   3),
  `Load-linked`   = round(summary(m_load)$concordance[1],   3),
  `Random-impact` = round(summary(m_impact)$concordance[1], 3)
))

show_tbl(mech_tab, "Mechanism split - HR per SD (top rows) and model concordance (bottom row)")
```

The bottom row adds each model's discrimination. The three are close,
but **random-impact is the lowest** at
`r round(summary(m_impact)$concordance[1], 3)`, below soft-tissue
(`r round(summary(m_soft)$concordance[1], 3)`) and load-linked
(`r round(summary(m_load)$concordance[1], 3)`). That's the direction the
negative-control logic predicts: the model ranks the load-relevant
injuries better than the random contact ones, because a random-impact
injury, a jammed finger, a poke in the eye, is by definition the least
driven by the workload, schedule and context the model is built from.

```{r trajectory, dependson="mechanism", fig.height=4.5, fig.width=7.5}
traj <- basehaz(m_soft, centered = FALSE) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  rename(cum_haz = hazard, game_number = time) %>%
  group_by(game_number) %>%
  summarise(cum_haz = mean(cum_haz), .groups = "drop") %>%   # average across season strata
  arrange(game_number)

haz_at <- function(g) traj$cum_haz[which.min(abs(traj$game_number - g))]

early_rate <- (haz_at(25) - haz_at(5))  / 20   # per-game hazard, games 5-25
late_rate  <- (haz_at(75) - haz_at(55)) / 20   # per-game hazard, games 55-75

ggplot(traj, aes(game_number, cum_haz)) +
  geom_line(colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(title = "Baseline cumulative hazard steepens as the season progresses",
       subtitle = paste0("Per-game hazard is ", sprintf("%.2f", late_rate / early_rate),
                         "x higher in games 55-75 than in games 5-25"),
       x = "Game number within season", y = "Cumulative baseline hazard") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

## What it shows

The mechanism split is the most important result in the thesis, and it
partly disconfirms my hypothesis. Chronic load carries a hazard ratio of
roughly `r round(summary(m_soft)$conf.int["z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D", 1], 1)`
for soft-tissue injury,
`r round(summary(m_load)$conf.int["z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D", 1], 1)` for
load-linked structural injury, and
`r round(summary(m_impact)$conf.int["z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D", 1], 1)` for
random-impact injury. If workload were purely causal, that third number
should collapse toward 1.0. It does not, if anything it is *higher* than
the soft-tissue figure. A player carrying heavy chronic load is about as
likely to break a finger as to tear a hamstring, relative to a low-load
player, and chronic load cannot plausibly *cause* a finger fracture. So
the chronic-load effect is substantially exposure and health-selection:
high-load players are on court more, and are selected for being fit
enough to sustain that load.

Acute load behaves differently, and this is the genuine signal. It is
elevated for the two load-relevant tiers (roughly
`r round(summary(m_soft)$conf.int["z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D", 1], 2)` for soft
tissue and
`r round(summary(m_load)$conf.int["z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D", 1], 2)` for
load-linked structural injury) but collapses to essentially 1.0 for
random impact
(`r round(summary(m_impact)$conf.int["z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D", 1], 2)`), the
pattern a real fatigue mechanism should produce, and about the cleanest
negative-control result I could have asked for. It is a smaller effect
than the chronic-load headline, but it is far better identified.

A caution I want on the record. I originally saw soft-tissue concordance
jump (0.693 → 0.744) when I first compared on-court distance to minutes,
and read it as external load being a *better predictor*. It turned out
to be a **tracking-data artefact**: DNP games carried a fake zero
distance that the carry-forward then leaked into the injury rows (fixed
in file 4). Corrected, load and minutes are **equivalent**, which is
exactly why I can report load as my exposure (it is the better
*construct*, what the body absorbed rather than what the coach chose)
without it changing a single result, and keep minutes as the Stage 1
robustness check. The lesson: distance is the right construct, but its
apparent *advantage* over minutes was a bug, not a finding.

The trajectory is the clean dynamic finding. Per-game baseline hazard is
`r sprintf("%.1f", late_rate / early_rate)` x steeper in games 55–75
than games 5–25.

Note: it is a property of the baseline hazard, not of any covariate
coefficient, which is precisely why Stage 2 found no covariate drifting.
The season gets more dangerous for everyone; it does not change how
workload acts. Those are different claims and only the survival framing
separates them.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Stage 6 - Out-of-sample validation

Everything above reports apparent performance, the model scored on the
same data it was fitted to, which is optimistic by construction. A model
with 24 covariates has ample opportunity to fit noise. So I hold data
out and score the frozen model on rows it has never seen, two
complementary ways:

-   **Temporal split**: train on 2021-22 … 2024-25, test on 2025-26.
    This is the operational question: trained on past seasons, does it
    work on a future one? It is how a rolling risk tool would actually
    be operationalised.
-   **Player-grouped 5-fold CV**: each fold holds out whole *players*.
    This is the fair test for repeated-measures data. A naive random row
    split would put LeBron's game 5 in training and his game 6 in test,
    and the model would score well by having memorised him rather than
    by having learned anything general.

Two Notes on the training data:

1.  Z-scores are computed on training rows only and then applied to test
    rows. Scaling on the pooled data would leak the test distribution
    into training.
2.  `strata(SEASON)` is dropped here. A stratified model has no baseline
    for a season it never saw, so it could not score 2025-26 at all.
    Discrimination only needs the linear predictor Xβ, which requires no
    baseline, so a common-baseline fit is both sufficient and necessary
    here.

```{r validation-setup, dependson="model-specs"}
zcols <- c("ROLLING_MIN_7D","ROLLING_MIN_28D","ACWR_MIN","ROLLING_GAMES_7D",
           "ROLLING_DIST_7D","ROLLING_DIST_28D","SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST","MIN",
           "PREV_GAME_MIN","PREV_2GAME_MIN",
           "ROLLING_LOAD_7D","ROLLING_LOAD_28D","ACWR_LOAD",
           "PREV_GAME_DISTANCE","PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE",
           "ROLLING_B2B_7D","ROLLING_B2B_28D","PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP_GAME_NUMBER",
           "TEAM_DAYS_REST","SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE","CAREER_GAMES_MISSED",
           "PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON","PCT_THROUGH_SEASON","HEIGHT_INCHES","WEIGHT")

# primary = the reported load model; minutes = the same spec with minutes swapped in,
# validated out of sample as the robustness check (both on the new-injury outcome).
specs <- list(
  primary = list(outcome = "event", terms = c(paste0("z_", c("ROLLING_LOAD_7D","ROLLING_LOAD_28D","ACWR_LOAD","ROLLING_GAMES_7D","PREV_GAME_DISTANCE","PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE")),
                                              "z_ROLLING_DIST_7D","z_ROLLING_DIST_28D","z_SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST",
                                              schedule_added, context_added)),
  minutes = list(outcome = "event", terms = c(paste0("z_", c("ROLLING_MIN_7D","ROLLING_MIN_28D","ACWR_MIN","ROLLING_GAMES_7D","PREV_GAME_MIN","PREV_2GAME_MIN")),
                                              "z_ROLLING_DIST_7D","z_ROLLING_DIST_28D","z_SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST",
                                              schedule_added, context_added))
)

# Standardise using TRAIN mean/sd only, then apply that same scaling to test.
add_z <- function(train, test, cols) {
  for (cc in cols) {
    m <- mean(train[[cc]], na.rm = TRUE); s <- sd(train[[cc]], na.rm = TRUE)
    train[[paste0("z_", cc)]] <- (train[[cc]] - m) / s
    test [[paste0("z_", cc)]] <- (test [[cc]] - m) / s
  }
  list(train = train, test = test)
}

# No season strata, so the risk score transfers to unseen seasons/players.
fit_spec <- function(data, spec) {
  coxph(as.formula(paste0("Surv(t_start, t_stop, ", spec$outcome, ") ~ ",
                          paste(spec$terms, collapse = " + "), " + cluster(PLAYER_ID)")),
        data = data, ties = "efron")
}

# concordance(Surv ~ x) treats larger x as LONGER survival; a Cox risk score is the
# opposite, so reverse = TRUE flips it back to the conventional C-index.
c_index <- function(fit, data, outcome) {
  d <- data
  d$.lp <- as.numeric(predict(fit, newdata = data, type = "lp"))
  concordance(as.formula(paste0("Surv(t_start, t_stop, ", outcome, ") ~ .lp")),
              data = d, reverse = TRUE)$concordance
}
```

```{r temporal-validation, dependson="validation-setup"}
test_season <- "2025-26"
tr0 <- cox %>% filter(SEASON != test_season)
te0 <- cox %>% filter(SEASON == test_season)

temporal <- map_dfr(names(specs), function(nm) {
  sp  <- specs[[nm]]
  sc  <- add_z(tr0, te0, zcols)
  fit <- fit_spec(sc$train, sp)
  tibble(model      = nm,
         apparent_C = round(c_index(fit, sc$train, sp$outcome), 4),
         temporal_C = round(c_index(fit, sc$test,  sp$outcome), 4))
})

show_tbl(temporal, paste0("Temporal validation - trained pre-", test_season,
                          ", tested on ", test_season))
```

```{r oos-calibration, dependson="temporal-validation"}
sc    <- add_z(tr0, te0, zcols)
fit_p <- fit_spec(sc$train, specs$primary)

calib_oos <- sc$test %>%
  mutate(risk = as.numeric(predict(fit_p, newdata = ., type = "lp"))) %>%
  filter(!is.na(risk)) %>%
  mutate(risk_group = ntile(risk, 5)) %>%      # 5 bands, not 10 - the test season is smaller
  group_by(risk_group) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), events = sum(event),
            event_rate_1k = round(1000 * sum(event) / n(), 1), .groups = "drop")

show_tbl(calib_oos, "Out-of-sample calibration in the held-out season (primary model)")
```

```{r player-cv, dependson="validation-setup"}
set.seed(42)
players <- tibble(PLAYER_ID = unique(cox$PLAYER_ID),
                  fold      = sample(rep(1:5, length.out = n_distinct(cox$PLAYER_ID))))
coxf <- cox %>% left_join(players, by = "PLAYER_ID")

player_cv <- map_dfr(names(specs), function(nm) {
  sp  <- specs[[nm]]
  oos <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(coxf))          # every row gets a score from a model blind to it
  for (k in 1:5) {
    tr  <- coxf %>% filter(fold != k)       # the other four folds' players
    idx <- which(coxf$fold == k)
    sc  <- add_z(tr, coxf[idx, ], zcols)
    fit <- fit_spec(sc$train, sp)
    oos[idx] <- as.numeric(predict(fit, newdata = sc$test, type = "lp"))
  }
  d <- coxf; d$.lp <- oos
  tibble(model = nm,
         player_cv_C = round(
           concordance(as.formula(paste0("Surv(t_start, t_stop, ", sp$outcome, ") ~ .lp")),
                       data = d, reverse = TRUE)$concordance, 4))
})

validation_summary <- temporal %>% left_join(player_cv, by = "model")
show_tbl(validation_summary, "Validation summary - apparent vs two out-of-sample estimates")
```

## What it shows

The gap is roughly **0.01 of concordance** on both models and under both
schemes. That is small, it says the model is not overfitted, and that
its apparent performance is close to what it would deliver on genuinely
new data.

Both out-of-sample schemes need to both return similar conclusions,
because they fail in different ways. The temporal split would expose a
model that only worked in the seasons it was trained on; the
player-grouped CV would expose one that had memorised specific players.

The `minutes` robustness spec lands right on top of the primary (load)
model out of sample - the held-out concordances are identical (see the
table). So the exposure choice, load or minutes, makes no difference to
how the model generalises, which is what I'd expect given they are
\~0.99 collinear.

Out-of-sample calibration holds too, observed injury rates in the
held-out season still climb across risk bands built from the frozen
model. The ranking transfers.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Conclusion

**1. Workload predicts injury timing, but much of that is exposure, not
fatigue.** Chronic load shows a large hazard ratio, but my negative
control shows it acts at least as strongly on random-impact injuries as
on soft-tissue ones. I would be overclaiming to present the chronic-load
HR as a causal fatigue effect, and the mechanism split is the evidence
that stops me.

**2. The genuine fatigue signal is acute load, and it is smaller.**
Acute 7-day load fades across the injury tiers in the way a causal
mechanism should.

**3. I report on-court load, but it is interchangeable with minutes -
and catching *why* mattered.** I use load because it is the better
construct (what the body absorbed, not what the coach chose), and the
whole model holds identically under a minutes robustness fit
(concordance `r round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 2)` either way,
chronic HR \~`r round(summary(m3)$conf.int["z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D", 1], 1)`
either way). An earlier version had load *out-predicting* minutes for
soft-tissue injury (0.693 → 0.744); that was a tracking-data bug, DNP
games leaking a fake zero distance, not a real edge. Distance is the
right idea, but in NBA public data total load ≈ minutes (r ≈ 0.99) and
the injurious high-speed component is unobserved, so the two are
equivalent.

**4. The season's danger is in the baseline, not the coefficients.**
Per-game baseline hazard is `r sprintf("%.1f", late_rate / early_rate)`
x steeper late season, while covariate effects stay proportional
throughout. Heavy chronic load is equally bad in October and April - the
background risk is what rises.

**5. Injury-proneness is real and largely unmeasured.** θ =
`r round(theta, 3)` implies a
`r round(exp(2 * qnorm(0.9) * sd_frail), 1)` x spread between the 90th
and 10th percentile of proneness after adjusting for everything I have.
Public data does not capture it.

## Limitations I want stated plainly

-   Health-gating is not fully solved. Point-in-time rest and
    back-to-back covariates read protective because coaches rest at-risk
    players. I mark them rather than interpret them, but I cannot remove
    the bias with observational data.
-   The outcome is an availability signal, not a diagnosis. Injuries
    come from official pre-game injury reports. I observe "listed Out
    with a reason", not a clinician's diagnosis, and reason text is
    inconsistent.
-   Concordance around 0.68 - 0.73 is a ceiling for public data. No GPS,
    no medical screening, no detailed training load. I'd frame this as
    establishing what public data *can* do rather than as a competitive
    predictive model.
-   The lagged in-game load terms cost coverage. Requiring two prior
    played games means a player's first two appearances each season
    cannot be scored, so the primary model fits
    `r format(m3$nevent, big.mark = ",")` new-injury events rather than
    the full `r format(sum(cox$event), big.mark = ",")`. Early-season
    injuries are the blind spot this introduces, a fair price for a
    prospective, correctly-signed load term.
-   Mechanism tiers involve judgement. I assign categories by regex on
    reason text. The three-tier split is defensible but not the only
    defensible one.
-   Five seasons, one league. Two are COVID-affected. Season strata
    handle the shape differences but cannot manufacture generalisability
    beyond the NBA
